title: How to Get Your Real Estate Investing License: A Step-by-Step Guide
excerpt: Wondering if you need a real estate license to invest — and how to get one? This guide breaks down the licensing process, costs, timelines, and when it actually makes sense for investors.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: how to get your real estate investing license
metaDescription: Learn how to get your real estate investing license step by step, including costs, timelines, and whether you actually need one as an investor.
metaKeywords: how to get your real estate investing license, real estate license for investors, should investors get licensed, real estate license requirements, wholesaling real estate license

sections.content: One of the most common questions new investors ask is whether they need a license — and if so, how to get your real estate investing license the right way. The honest answer is that most investors do not legally need one. But getting licensed can open doors that would otherwise stay closed: access to MLS listings, the ability to earn commissions, and a deeper understanding of deals. If you are serious about growing a long-term investing business, it is worth understanding exactly what a license involves. For a broader look at building your operation, check out the [Scaling a Real Estate Investing Business: Complete Guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/scaling-real-estate-investing-business).
Do Real Estate Investors Actually Need a License?

Let's clear this up first. There is no such thing as a specific "real estate investing license." What most people mean when they ask this question is: should I get a standard real estate salesperson or broker license as an investor? The answer depends on your strategy. Wholesalers, buy-and-hold landlords, and fix-and-flip investors can all operate without a license. However, if you plan to represent buyers or sellers, earn commissions, or access MLS data directly, you will need a license. If you are just getting started, the [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) is a great place to understand your options before committing to the licensing path.
Step-by-Step: How to Get Your Real Estate License as an Investor
The licensing process is handled at the state level, so requirements vary. That said, the core steps are nearly identical across all 50 states. Here is a realistic breakdown of what to expect.
Step 1: Meet Your State's Basic Requirements

items: Must be at least 18 or 19 years old depending on the state
Must have a high school diploma or GED
Must be a legal U.S. resident
Must pass a background check (felony convictions may disqualify you in some states)

sections.content: Step 2: Complete Pre-Licensing Education

Every state requires a certain number of classroom or online hours before you can sit for the exam. Requirements range from 40 hours in states like Michigan to 180 hours in Texas and California. Most states fall somewhere between 60 and 90 hours. You can complete coursework through in-person schools, online platforms like Real Estate Express or Colibri, or community colleges. Budget $100 to $500 for this step. Online options tend to be cheaper and let you study at your own pace, which is ideal if you are already active in the market.
Step 3: Pass the State Licensing Exam

After finishing your coursework, you register for the state exam through a testing provider like Pearson VUE or PSI. The exam typically has two parts: a national portion covering general real estate principles and a state-specific portion covering local laws and practices. Passing scores vary but usually fall in the 70 to 75 percent range. The exam fee runs between $40 and $100 depending on your state. Many candidates do not pass on the first attempt, so give yourself two to four weeks to study using practice exams before scheduling your test date.

Pro Tip: Focus your study time on math questions and state-specific contract law. These two areas trip up the most first-time test takers. Most online prep courses include timed practice exams that closely mirror the real test — use them daily in your final week of prep.
Step 4: Find a Sponsoring Broker

Here is the part most people overlook. In every state, a newly licensed salesperson must work under a licensed broker. You cannot simply activate your license and go solo right away. As an investor, this does not mean you have to become a traditional agent. Many investors hang their license with an investor-friendly or flat-fee brokerage that charges a monthly desk fee instead of taking a commission split. Some brokerages charge as little as $50 to $100 per month, which makes this very manageable. Interview several brokers and ask specifically about their policy for investor-agents who are primarily doing their own deals.
Step 5: Submit Your Application and Pay State Fees

Once you pass the exam and secure a sponsoring broker, you submit your license application to your state's real estate commission. Application fees range from $50 to $350. Many states also require errors and omissions (E&O) insurance, which typically runs $300 to $600 per year and may be covered through your sponsoring brokerage. Expect the full process — from starting your coursework to holding an active license — to take between two and six months depending on your state and your study pace.
What Does a License Actually Cost?
The Real Benefits for Active Investors

Beyond just checking a box, a real estate license gives investors a genuine edge. Direct MLS access means you can pull comps, track days on market, and spot price reductions without relying on an agent. In active investing markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), being able to move on a deal the same day it hits the market can be the difference between landing it and losing it. Licensed investors can also earn a buyer's agent commission when purchasing properties, which effectively reduces acquisition costs by 2 to 3 percent per deal.

"Getting licensed was the best business decision I made as an investor. I saved over $18,000 in commissions in my first year alone — that money went straight back into buying more deals." — Active investor and licensed agent in the Dallas market
When a License May Not Be Worth It

If your strategy is focused purely on wholesaling, you may not need a license at all. Wholesalers assign contracts rather than buying and reselling properties, which generally does not require a license in most states — though regulations are tightening in some markets. Check out [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) to understand the legal landscape before you decide. If deal volume is your priority right now, the time you would spend studying for a license might be better spent building your pipeline and [refining your disposition strategies](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/wholesale-disposition-strategies) to close faster.
How Licensing Fits Into Building a Bigger Business

If you are looking to scale, a license can support your growth in meaningful ways. Licensed investors can build a team more effectively because they understand both sides of the transaction. As you grow, you will face decisions about [when to hire an acquisitions manager](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/acquisitions-manager-real-estate) and how to [build SOPs for your real estate business](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/sops-real-estate-business) so deals flow consistently. Having a license in-house reduces friction on both the buy and sell side, which matters a lot when you are doing volume. It also adds credibility with sellers, banks, and private lenders.

Pro Tip: Before you spend months studying for your license, run the numbers on your current deals. Use the free [Deal Calculator at aiwholesail.com](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to estimate how much you are paying in agent commissions per deal. If that number exceeds your first-year licensing costs, getting licensed will pay for itself quickly.
Quick Summary: Your Licensing Roadmap

items: Confirm your state's specific hour requirements and fees (check your state real estate commission website)
Enroll in a state-approved pre-licensing course — online is fine
Study for and pass your state licensing exam (national + state sections)
Find an investor-friendly sponsoring broker with low monthly fees
Submit your application and secure E&O insurance
Activate your license and start using MLS access on your very next deal
